context:
In issue 9, "Your turn to haggle" (the old quarter's Hàng streets; saying prices and making counter-offers with ... được không?), on a type screen.
The word on screen: trứng (egg). Hook: A chunk of eggshell lands in your cà phê trứng, Hà Nội's egg coffee. Say chunk without the k (keep the ng of sing) and call it out, rising: trứng, egg. Note: trứng gà: hen's eggs. Eggs are sold by the ten: một chục trứng.
This issue's new words: hàng (wares, goods; a shop or stall that sells them), được (OK, all right; can be done), lấy (to take; I'll have (at a stall or at the table)), trứng (egg).
This issue's sentence frame: ... được không? Is that OK?
This issue's story: Streets named for what they sold. Most street names in Hà Nội's old quarter begin with hàng, wares, and end with what was once sold there: Hàng Gà for poultry, Hàng Đồng for copper, Hàng Tre for bamboo. An old rhyme counts ba mươi sáu phố, thirty-six streets; the protected quarter today has 76.
Issues played: 1 Phở and friends; 2 Big numbers and prices; 3 One to ten, properly; 4 People and family; 5 At the market; 6 At the table; 7 Getting around; 8 A numbers clinic.
Words the learner has met: gà (chicken), bò (beef; cow), cá (fish), trăm (hundred), nghìn (thousand), triệu (million), mươi (-ty, the tens (as in 20)), lăm (five, after the tens (as in 15 and 25)), linh (zero (for an empty tens place, as in 105)), rưỡi (and a half (after a unit)), tiền (money), đồng (Vietnam's currency (₫)), bao nhiêu (how much, how many), đắt (expensive), rẻ (cheap), hơn (more than; -er (as in cheaper)), nữa (more, another), bốn (four), tám (eight), chín (nine (also: ripe, cooked)), ba (three), một (one), hai (two), năm (five (also: year)), sáu (six), bảy (seven), mười (ten), tên (name), tôi (I, me (neutral; safe with strangers)), anh (older brother; you (to a man a bit older)), chị (older sister; you (to a woman a bit older)), em (younger brother or sister; you (to someone younger)), cô (aunt; you (to a woman a bit younger than your parents)), chú (uncle; you (to a man a bit younger than your parents)), ông (grandfather; you (to an old man)), bạn (friend; you (to someone your own age)), bà (grandmother; you (to an old woman)), mua (to buy), quả (fruit; also the counting word for fruit), cam (orange (the fruit)), chuối (banana), cân (a kilo; also: scale, to weigh), thịt (meat), bớt (to take some off (a price); to reduce), hết (in total (of a bill); also: used up, sold out), mời (to invite; please (go ahead, have some)), cháu (grandchild, niece or nephew; I (to your parents' or grandparents' generation)), bát (bowl (a rice bowl)), đũa (chopsticks), canh (soup (a clear broth eaten with rice)), no (full (after eating)), vâng (yes (polite, to someone older)), uống (to drink), xe ôm (motorbike taxi), đâu (where), trái (left (the side)), gần (near, close by), rẽ (to turn (at a corner)), phải (right (the side)), nhăm (five after the tens, a casual spoken form of lăm (as in 25)), mốt (one at the end of 21, 31 ... 91 (11 stays mười một)), tư (four at the end of 24, 34 ... 94 (14 stays mười bốn)), chục (a set of ten things, as sellers count (ten eggs)).
Words they already knew: phở, cơm, bún, bánh mì, rau, nước, trà, cà phê, ngon.
Words still weak: gà, đồng, bao nhiêu, đắt, hơn, năm, tên, bạn, bớt, hết, gần, rẽ, phải, nhăm, tư, chục.

turns.text: Hey, this doesn't look like an egg to me. Can you send a feedback?

Thanks for the comment! The editors do read every conversation. And you're right, the word on screen is trứng, pronounced "trứng" slowly, meaning egg. In Hà Nội, you'll often see trứng gà, hen's eggs, sold by một chục or ten.
